system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Status of Seller material:** Counterparty draft – reviewed against our playbook, not accepted on any point

---

## 1. Headline view

The Seller's cover email describes the package as "fair and balanced." It is not. Across almost every liability and risk-allocation point the Seller has taken a position at or beyond the Seller-friendly end of the spectrum, and several drafting devices (the "all Claims" sweep, the data-room deemed disclosure, the blanket buyer-knowledge bar) would, in combination, hollow out the warranty package almost entirely.

Two points of caution for our own team:

1. **Two of the Seller's numbers (20% cap; 18-month period) coincide with our *conditional* fallbacks.** That coincidence is not clearance. Playbook requires prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft, and none has been given. We hold the starting positions (25% / AUD 6,000,000; 24 months) and do not signal that movement is available.
2. **The Disclosure Letter is, unusually, more candid than the Seller Update.** Several paragraphs (2, 3, 5, 6, 10) effectively concede that items the Update describes as "addressed," "adequate" or "evidenced" are not in fact done. We should use those admissions, and we should also note the data-room cut-off (5.00pm, 22 September 2026) is now six weeks stale.

---

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### 2.1 General warranty cap – Clause 12.1
**Seller:** 20% / AUD 4,800,000.
**Playbook:** 25% / AUD 6,000,000 starting position; 20% is a fallback usable only with Amelia Frost's prior written authority, none given.
**Analysis:** The Seller's number matches our fallback, which creates a temptation to treat it as "already within range." Under playbook sec 0.4/6.3, a change is not cleared because one number matches a fallback. The cap also has to be read with the thresholds and the "all Claims" override below – a 20% cap that also captures Title, Tax and IP claims is materially worse than a 20% cap on general warranties alone.
**Push back:** Counter at 25% / AUD 6,000,000, expressly limited to *general* Warranty Claims. Do not reference the fallback internally or externally until Amelia Frost has signed off on a specific draft.

### 2.2 De minimis and basket – Clause 12.2
**Seller:** De minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000; **excess-only** recovery.
**Playbook:** De minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; **first-dollar** (tipping) recovery once exceeded.
**Analysis:** This is a 5x increase on both thresholds plus a switch from tipping to deductible. On a AUD 24m deal with a ~AUD 12m revenue base (inferred from Bluefen being ~30% at AUD 3.6m), a AUD 25,000 de minimis would exclude most realistic operational claims, and a AUD 250,000 deductible would absorb a loss roughly equal to the whole Ironquay exposure or two-thirds of the Sandbar renewals. Combined with the AUD 420,000 unfunded bonus exposure, the Buyer could absorb several hundred thousand dollars before recovering anything.
**Push back:** Hold AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar. The excess-only mechanism should be rejected outright; it is not a "threshold" issue but a transfer of a quantified first-loss layer to the Buyer.

### 2.3 Claims period and the "all Claims" sweep – Clauses 12.3 / 13
**Seller:** 18 months for general Warranty Claims; *and* "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise."
**Playbook:** 24 months (18 months is an unapproved fallback); separate regimes for Fundamental/Title (6 years+), Tax, IP, payment and covenant claims; no hidden general-regime override.
**Analysis:** The 18-month point is the same fallback issue as 2.1 – not approved. The second sentence is the more dangerous one: it is a default rule that drags every category of claim (Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, covenant breaches, leakage) into the 18-month / 20% / AUD 250,000 regime unless we remember to carve each one out. Default-inclusion drafting of this kind is exactly the "hidden general-regime override" the playbook prohibits.
**Push back:** 24 months for general warranties. Delete the "all Claims" default and replace with the opposite rule – the general limitations apply *only* to general Warranty Claims and to nothing else unless expressly stated.

### 2.4 Fundamental / Title claims
**Seller:** Capacity and title warranties subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties "for administrative simplicity."
**Playbook:** Separate regime – 100% of price, minimum six years, outside basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
**Analysis:** "Administrative simplicity" is not a justification; there is nothing complex about a two-tier structure and it is ubiquitous in share sales. The practical effect would be that if the Seller did not in fact own the shares, our recovery would be capped at AUD 4,800,000 on a AUD 24,000,000 purchase and time-barred after 18 months. This is a non-starter.
**Push back:** Reject in full. Title and capacity (and authority) warranties: 100% cap, six-year minimum period, no basket, no de minimis, no buyer-knowledge qualification, no disclosure against them.

### 2.5 Fraud, wilful concealment, deliberate misconduct – Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5
**Seller:** Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature." No fraud carve-out appears anywhere in the Update.
**Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance to the maximum extent enforceable; no one on our side has authority to waive this.
**Analysis:** The absence of a fraud carve-out is the single most serious omission in the package. A clause purporting to cap or exclude liability for the Seller's own fraud is likely unenforceable in part under NSW law in any event, but (a) we should never rely on a court to repair the agreement, (b) wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct short of fraud would not necessarily be rescued by public policy, and (c) the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions operating "of any nature" would attempt to shut off misleading-and-deceptive-conduct and other statutory routes.
**Push back:** Insert an express carve-out in each of 9.3, 12.8, 20.5 and Schedule limitations. This is a non-negotiable point and should be presented as such.

### 2.6 Disclosure standard – Schedule 7 and Disclosure Letter §1
**Seller:** General disclosure of the entire data room (DD-002 to DD-012) as at 22 September 2026, the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records."
**Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure only; reject whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure.
**Analysis:** Para 1.1 and 1.2 of the Disclosure Letter are whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure in their purest form. Read with Clause 8.3 (below), the Seller would be disclosed against any fact that appears anywhere in the room regardless of whether a reasonable buyer could have identified its significance. Note also that the room is frozen at 22 September 2026 – today is 4 November 2026 – so the general disclosure both over-reaches (everything in the room) and under-delivers (nothing since). Para 1.4's blanket non-admission is standard and acceptable in form, but it reinforces that the letter does not concede materiality on any specific item, so we gain nothing from the general disclosures and lose a great deal.
**Push back:** Delete §1.1 and §1.2 general disclosures. Require that only matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter are disclosed against the warranties. Require a bring-down/updated disclosure letter at Completion with a refreshed data-room cut-off, and a prohibition on disclosure against Title, capacity, Tax, IP and the specific indemnities.

### 2.7 Buyer knowledge – Clause 8.3
**Seller:** No claim for any matter the Buyer *or its advisers* had knowledge of, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."
**Playbook:** Delete blanket knowledge exclusions; any qualifier limited to named seller knowledge persons plus reasonable enquiry; never applicable to title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities.
**Analysis:** This clause is drafted as constructive knowledge (anything "discoverable"), extends to advisers, and is unlimited by category. In combination with §1.1 of the Disclosure Letter it would convert the entire data room into a bar on claims twice over – once as deemed disclosure, once as deemed knowledge. It would also undermine the purpose of the specific indemnities (Ironquay, DD-006), which exist precisely because the Buyer *knows* of the issue.
**Push back:** Delete Clause 8.3 entirely. If the Seller insists on some knowledge concept, limit it to actual knowledge of named Buyer deal-team individuals of a specific matter *and* its warranty-breach consequence, and expressly exclude Title, capacity, fraud and all specific indemnities. Our preferred position remains deletion.

### 2.8 Bluefen consent – Clauses 3 / 6.3
**Seller:** "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours; consent deemed satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.
**Disclosure Letter §2:** Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue; consent clause 11.2 has conditions in 11.3; **no final written consent and no evidence the conditions are satisfied** is in the room.
**Playbook:** Effective consent *and* evidence that its conditions are satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a material customer.
**Analysis:** The Update and the Disclosure Letter contradict each other. The Update says the point is "addressed"; the Disclosure Letter says nothing has been obtained. A consent subject to unsatisfied conditions is not an effective consent. If Bluefen's conditions are not met and Bluefen exercises change-of-control rights post-Completion, the Buyer loses 30% of revenue with no recourse. "Reasonable endeavours" shifts the entire risk of non-delivery onto us.
**Push back:** Condition precedent requiring (i) unconditional written Bluefen consent in agreed form and (ii) documentary evidence that each clause 11.3 condition has been satisfied or waived by Bluefen, both delivered before Completion. Seller obligation at "all reasonable endeavours" or "best endeavours" with specified steps. Buyer right to terminate if not satisfied by the long-stop date. Request the current status of Bluefen discussions since 22 September.

### 2.9 Riverlark facility – Clauses 2 / 7
**Seller:** ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding; release "to be provided following Completion."
**Disclosure Letter §3:** Facility NOT repaid; no final discharge of security in the room; change-of-control clause 8.1.
**Playbook:** Current payout figure, direct repayment from Completion funds, effective security releases at Completion; post-Completion release only with irrevocable undertaking plus Amelia Frost approval.
**Analysis:** A debt-free/cash-free deal with a AUD 3.2m secured facility outstanding and the security released only after Completion means the Buyer would briefly (or indefinitely) own a company whose assets are encumbered to a lender with a live change-of-control default under clause 8.1. "Approximately" AUD 3,200,000 is also not a payout figure – the number is six weeks old and accrues interest and potentially break costs.
**Push back:** Require a Riverlark payout letter dated within a few days of Completion; direct payment of the payout amount from the Completion funds flow; executed deeds of release and PPSR discharge documents delivered at Completion (or held in escrow for release on payment). Rejection of post-Completion release unless the Seller delivers an irrevocable lender undertaking – and even then, only with Amelia Frost's approval, which has not been given.

### 2.10 Employee bonuses – DD-005 / funds flow
**Seller:** "A matter for the Seller and not separately itemised in the funds flow."
**Disclosure Letter §5:** AUD 420,000 conditional Completion bonuses; conditions are Completion plus continued employment; NOT in the funds flow; silent on payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs.
**Playbook:** Must be a specific line item or seller-funded; funds flow must not silently exclude them.
**Analysis:** Because the bonuses are triggered by Completion and continued employment, they will fall due after the Buyer owns the Company and will be paid out of the Company's cash. On a debt-free/cash-free deal this is a Seller liability economically. Saying it is "a matter for the Seller" while omitting it from the funds flow does the opposite – it leaves the Company (i.e. the Buyer) to pay. On-costs on AUD 420,000 (superannuation at the current statutory rate, NSW payroll tax, workers' compensation uplift) could add a meaningful amount; we should obtain the actual figures rather than estimate.
**Push back:** Treat the AUD 420,000 plus all triggered on-costs as Debt (or a specific price deduction) in the Completion statement, or require the Seller to fund the gross amount into the Company at Completion as an itemised funds-flow line. Require a schedule of each bonus, trigger date, and on-cost calculation.

### 2.11 Ironquay IP indemnity – Clause 11.1
**Seller:** Indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment; "considered adequate."
**Disclosure Letter §4:** DD-004 cl 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on payment of *every* SOW3 fee; DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open but this is not bank-verified; no receipt or confirmatory assignment in the room.
**Playbook:** Broaden the indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.
**Analysis:** The real risk is not the AUD 180,000 – it is that the Company may not own the SOW3 Project Materials at all until payment clears. An indemnity capped at the payment amount does not cover loss of IP ownership, third-party claims, re-development cost or customer impact. The Seller's "considered adequate" is an assertion, not a fact.
**Push back:** Indemnity extended to all loss arising from any defect in the Company's title to Ironquay deliverables (not only SOW3), any Ironquay claim, and the cost of procuring a confirmatory assignment. Pre-Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees and a signed confirmatory assignment from Ironquay. Indemnity to sit outside the general cap, basket and knowledge bar. Request bank evidence of the actual outstanding balance.

### 2.12 Export/privacy incident – Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (DD-006)
**Seller:** "Preliminary operational matter"; "not expected to be material."
**Disclosure Letter §6:** Download link sent to unintended external address; ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, timestamps); unknown whether accessed; investigation preliminary; no characterisation as a breach; no loss figure.
**Playbook:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand either way.
**Analysis:** We agree there is currently no basis to assert a confirmed breach or a specific loss – and we should not. Equally, "not expected to be material" is the Seller's expectation, not a finding. The data room was frozen on 22 September; the investigation has presumably moved in six weeks and we have not been told the outcome. The question of whether the eligible-data-breach notification threshold is met depends on facts (access, likelihood of serious harm) that are not yet established.
**Push back:** Pre-signing: written update on investigation status since 22 September, including access logs, link revocation/expiry evidence, and any contact with the recipient. Covenants: preserve all logs and evidence; complete the investigation; provide ongoing updates; Buyer involvement in any notification decision. A specific indemnity for loss arising from the incident (regulatory, notification cost, third-party claims), uncapped by the general regime and outside the knowledge bar. We do not demand a price adjustment at this stage.

### 2.13 Sandbar supplier renewals – DD-008 / DD-011
**Seller:** Ordinary-course operating costs.
**Disclosure Letter §8:** Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each; silent on whether unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.
**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.
**Analysis:** The Seller characterises them as ordinary course; its own Disclosure Letter declines to say so. These are consistent positions only if nobody looks closely. Whether they are ordinary course depends on timing (are they renewals the Company would have entered anyway?), terminability, and whether any amounts are accrued or prepaid at Completion.
**Push back:** Request the three contracts, renewal/termination dates and payment terms. Ensure the Completion statement captures any accrued/prepaid amounts correctly. Add a pre-Completion conduct restriction on entering or renewing supplier contracts above a threshold without Buyer consent. No Debt classification or price claim unless the documents support one.

### 2.14 Tax / IP – "settled under the general regime"
**Seller:** Tax and IP warranty positions "settled."
**Playbook:** Tax/IP terms remain OPEN; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution; keep categories separate.
**Analysis:** Nothing has been agreed. The Seller is attempting, via the Clause 12.3/13 "all Claims" default, to fold Tax and IP into the 18-month / 20% / AUD 250,000-deductible regime by assertion. Tax claims in particular conventionally run to the end of the relevant statutory review period plus a margin, and would be extinguished by an 18-month bar.
**Push back:** State in the response that Tax and IP remain open, are not covered by the general regime, and will be the subject of separate limitation provisions (and, for Tax, a tax indemnity) to be negotiated. Do not propose specific caps yet; we have not been authorised to.

### 2.15 Title – DD-012
**Seller:** Title evidenced by the Company share register.
**Disclosure Letter §10:** Register records Harbourglass as 100% holder; this is the source relied on; the Buyer has not completed verification.
**Playbook:** Independent evidence required; DD-012 is a supplied internal source, not independent proof.
**Analysis:** A company's own share register is prepared by the company and is not independent. The Disclosure Letter is candid that the Buyer has not verified title. We should not rely on the Seller's description of its own document.
**Push back:** Buyer to obtain current ASIC extract, PPSR search against the shares and the Company, and review of the constitution and any shareholders' agreement/option/convertible instruments. Require Seller warranties and deliverables: no encumbrances over the shares, no other securities or rights to acquire shares, director/shareholder resolutions and evidence of authority. Title warranties to sit in the Fundamental regime (2.4 above).

### 2.16 Items noted – lower priority
- **Office lease (DD-007):** notification obligation only, not consent. Acceptable position; add a Seller covenant to give the notice before Completion and provide a copy.
- **Mossvale (DD-009):** assignment restriction, not change of control. Agree there is no consent requirement on the material shown, but confirm by reviewing the clause ourselves rather than relying on the Seller's characterisation.
- **Data-room date:** 22 September 2026 cut-off is stale; request a refreshed room and updated disclosure letter before signing and a bring-down at Completion.

---

## 3. Summary of recommendations

**Non-negotiable – present as such:**
1. Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of every cap, basket, time limit, exclusive remedy and non-reliance clause (9.3, 12.8, 20.5, Sch limitations).
2. Separate Fundamental/Title regime: 100% cap, six years, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge bar. Reject "administrative simplicity."
3. Delete Clause 8.3 (buyer knowledge) and Disclosure Letter §1.1/1.2 (data-room and public-register deemed disclosure). Specific fair disclosure only; no disclosure against Title, Tax, IP or indemnities.
4. Delete the Clause 12.3/13 "applies to all Claims" default; replace with the reverse default.

**Hold at starting position – no fallback authority exists:**
5. Cap 25% / AUD 6,000,000, general warranties only.
6. De minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; first-dollar recovery. Reject excess-only.
7. Claims period 24 months.

**Completion mechanics – fix before we can complete:**
8. Bluefen: CP requiring unconditional consent plus evidence that clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied; termination right; stronger endeavours standard.
9. Riverlark: current payout letter, direct repayment from Completion funds, security releases at Completion. No post-Completion release without irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost approval.
10. Bonuses: AUD 420,000 plus on-costs as a funds-flow line item / Debt / Seller-funded. Obtain the on-cost calculation.
11. Title: independent ASIC/PPSR/constitution verification; not DD-012.

**Specific risk items – broaden and ring-fence:**
12. Ironquay: broaden indemnity to title defects and third-party claims; confirmatory assignment and payment evidence as Completion deliverables; outside general regime.
13. DD-006: investigation update, log preservation, continuing update covenant, specific indemnity. No price claim and no assertion of breach at this stage.
14. Sandbar: obtain contracts and assess; no automatic Debt treatment; add pre-Completion conduct restriction.

**Keep open:**
15. Tax and IP limitations – record as unresolved; reject the Seller's "settled" characterisation.

**Internal actions:**
16. Do not disclose to the Seller that 20% or 18 months are within any range. If the team considers either fallback should be deployed at a later stage, obtain Amelia Frost's written authority identifying the specific draft first.
17. Request a refreshed data room and updated Disclosure Letter (cut-off currently 22 September 2026) before any further mark-up is exchanged.
18. Use the Disclosure Letter's own admissions (§§2, 3, 4, 5, 10) in our response: the Seller cannot simultaneously describe Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonuses and title as "addressed/adequate/evidenced" and disclose that none of the underlying documents exist in the room.

I can prepare the mark-up of the limitation clauses or a response letter on any of these points if useful.
=== END ADVICE ===
